arc: The forms assembled in Primitives acquire motion, then become surfaces and boundaries a visitor can use. A small timed study introduces interpolation and sine without requiring a theory of waves; later halls distinguish path, pivot, hierarchy and input. The student finishes with a deliberate transformation rule whose visible and physical consequences can be compared.

halls.title: Give a familiar cube a rhythm
halls.storyboard: Before the four pickup demonstrations, the student recognises the cube assembled in Primitives and watches translation, rotation and scale arrive one at a time. In a small companion study, they retain the created cube reference, accumulate elapsed seconds and drive height and size between two limits, adding a timed turn. The room, display and collection behaviour are supplied. A short sine comparison keeps the endpoints and duration while changing arrival speed; its range is explained now, its circular meaning later. The student leaves with an animation they can reuse deliberately.
halls.storyboard_short: Use four pickup demonstrations. Reuse the created cube reference. Teach elapsed seconds, bounded height/size interpolation and a timed turn. Compare sine arrival speed at equal endpoints and duration; explain its range. Supply room, readout and collection. Carry reusable animation. Keep the museum encounter linear; place sine in the companion study. Defer circular meaning.
learns: elapsed time and interpolation
usable sine cycle
halls.carries: A timed position, turn and size rule.
halls.review_note: Keep the linear museum encounter and place the sine comparison in the student study; the older intent still postpones all sine.

halls.title: Make a surface reach
halls.storyboard: The student crosses the moving cube, growing support and turning plank, bringing the animation operations from the pickup study. At the adjustable landing they hold the plank's motion fixed and move the destination, then use their known endpoint calculation to propose a crossing that reaches both banks. A prepared physical deck supplies collision and rider carrying; the learner controls its route and records its displacement. They discover that animating a surface and transporting a supported body require an explicit connection. A crossing specification, including its fixed references, travels onward.
halls.storyboard_short: Use moving cube, growing support, turning plank and adjustable landing. Reuse animation and endpoint calculations; hold plank motion fixed while moving the destination. Teach surface motion versus carried displacement. Supply banks, controls and physical deck with rider adapter. Carry a crossing specification with fixed references. Open: choose the smallest supported deck interface before drafting code.
learns: surface motion and carried displacement
halls.carries: A crossing with explicit endpoints and support.
halls.review_note: Choose the smallest supported deck interface before writing code; inspect source rather than teaching the whole transport script.

halls.title: Choose the journey between endpoints
halls.storyboard: Seven carrier journeys separate sideways, upward and forward travel before combining directions. Reusing positions, lists and interpolation, the student describes a short route as waypoints in one named frame, then compares visiting those waypoints with travelling straight to the final destination. The prepared carrier accepts consecutive target positions and supplies rider detection; a simple marker can preview the same route without carrying anyone. Subtraction gives each leg, and dividing a nonzero leg by its length separates direction from distance. The student carries a route generator whose endpoint does not conceal its intermediate journey.
halls.storyboard_short: Use seven carrier journeys. Reuse positions, lists and interpolation. Teach waypoints in one frame, leg subtraction and direction = leg/length for nonzero legs. Compare waypoint travel with the direct route. Supply carrier, rider connection and preview marker. Carry a route generator preserving intermediate travel. Open: choose marker preview or visitor carrying; carrying needs the preceding deck interface.
learns: waypoint traversal
direction separated from distance
halls.carries: A reusable waypoint route.
halls.review_note: Agree whether the first student route carries the visitor or only the preview marker; the former needs the deck interface from the preceding lesson.

halls.title: Turn around a chosen centre
halls.storyboard: At the blades and the marked cubes, the student follows an end while its centre stays fixed. With positions, functions and a timed angle available, they make a small arm from a centre and an offset, then rotate the offset around a named axis before adding the centre back. A supplied angle display and physical ride let them compare their construction with the larger encounter. Reversing two turns at the composition workbench tests order; the hinge offers a quiet return. The reusable result is a pivoted construction, distinct from moving the whole object.
halls.storyboard_short: Use blades, marked cubes and composition workbench. Reuse positions, functions and timed angles. Teach pivoted construction: rotate an offset around a named axis, then add its centre. Reverse two turns to test order. Supply angle display and physical ride; retain the hinge as a quiet return. Carry pivoted construction distinct from whole-object motion. Defer full rotated arrays and ride physics.
learns: axis and pivot
order of rotations
halls.carries: A function placing a point around a pivot.
halls.review_note: Keep axis-angle construction small; do not make all rotated arrays and ride physics prerequisites.

halls.title: Choose what the scale reaches
halls.storyboard: Taking the bottle enlarges the room while the visitor retains their size. The student brings uniform scale and a pivoted arrangement, then groups a small set of their own forms under one created parent and scales that parent beside an unchanged reference doorway. The existing room, bottle and relocation mechanism are supplied for the encounter. They compare scaled dimensions with scaled distances between children, and identify the separate operation that moves the visitor onto the table. A grouped construction with a clearly bounded scale becomes useful for later arrays and assemblies.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the bottle enlarging the room around an unchanged visitor. Reuse uniform scale and pivoted forms. Teach parent-child transforms through one created group beside a fixed doorway; compare dimensions and child spacing. Supply room, bottle and relocation; distinguish relocation from scaling. Carry a bounded grouped construction. Open: choose the small composition.
learns: parent-child transforms
halls.carries: A group that scales against a fixed reference.
halls.review_note: Decide the small grouped composition; do not require rebuilding the room, food or player relocation.

halls.title: Let proximity become an input
halls.storyboard: The slats open, the low lattice loses cells, and nearby blocks shrink. Reusing distance and interpolation, the student makes one small block respond to the supplied visitor position: convert distance to a bounded fraction, then use it to choose a size while keeping the base on the floor. The prepared body query and matching collision update are explained as inputs and outputs. Walking away distinguishes a reversible response from the lattice's retained removal. The learner takes forward a proximity function and the habit of asking which state an interaction keeps.
halls.storyboard_short: Use opening slats, retained lattice removal and shrinking blocks. Reuse distance and interpolation. Teach clamped distance-to-size mapping on one adjacent block, keeping its base grounded. Supply visitor-position query and matching collision updater with explicit inputs/outputs. Compare walking away with retained removal. Carry a proximity function and state distinction; keep carving infrastructure supplied.
learns: clamped input mapping
current response versus retained change
halls.carries: A bounded proximity-to-size function.
halls.review_note: Student block should sit beside the encounter; carving and visitor-recognition infrastructure remain supplied.

halls.title: Compose an opening through time
halls.storyboard: Beside the timed pushers, turning slabs and growers, the student predicts when a space becomes available and compares that prediction with the final airlock. They already have timed and proximity-driven transforms, so they compose a small pair of leaves whose position, angle and size receive different parts of one opening fraction. The doorway frame, occupancy input and physical leaf wrapper are supplied. Holding an intermediate pose makes clearance inspectable. No new syntax is necessary: the outcome is an authored transformation sequence that makes a usable opening, ready to be repeated across an array.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the level-ground timed pushers, slabs, growers and airlock. Reuse timed/proximity transforms. Compose two leaves whose position, angle and size share one opening fraction; hold an intermediate pose to inspect clearance. Supply frame, occupancy input and physical leaf wrapper. Carry an authored opening sequence toward arrays. Require no new syntax; discard obsolete pit/death framing.
learns: composed transforms from one control
halls.carries: An opening sequence with inspectable intermediate poses.
supplied: occupancy signal and physical leaf wrapper
halls.review_note: The current hall is a level-ground timed study; obsolete pit/death prose must not determine the exercise.

arc: PROPOSED. Keep an address while changing what its value asks a receiver to do. Return to Trace’s list and Transformation’s positioned body; extend a small occupancy record into a plane and a volume with explicit storage conventions. Then let an address choose a tile’s turn, give the same image another support, and let a clock read a score. Occupancy, orientation and musical events remain different kinds of data. Carry the read/write operation and declared readers into Colour and Tiling; automatic transport between museum exhibits is not assumed.

halls.title: Keep a place when its occupant leaves
halls.storyboard: The row loses a cube without closing its gap; the nearby grid lets the student locate another absence with two indices. Bringing Trace’s list and loop and Transformation’s positioned body, they begin with four slots, then extend the same read/write operation to a small grid. Follow the installed convention, grid_data[x][z], and keep occupancy values separate from visible-node references and spacing. A named display adapter and collection event are supplied. The student empties a chosen slot, changes the spacing and explains why the other addresses remain. They carry the occupancy record and its reader. Molnár’s retained departures offer an optional next experiment; the changing floor remains an encounter with the physical consequence of an empty place.
halls.storyboard_short: Use row and indexed grid. Reuse Trace list/loop and positioned bodies. Teach retained slots, then grid_data[x][z]; separate occupancy, node reference and spacing. Supply display adapter/collection event. Check: empty one slot, vary spacing, preserve addresses. Carry record + reader. Optional: stored Molnár departures. Floor writer stays an encounter. Open: reduced learner binding; Array tutorial absent.
learns: read/write a retained slot
two-index addressing in the installed x/z convention
occupancy value versus visible object reference
halls.carries: A small occupancy record and an explicit address-to-display reader
supplied: named display adapter and collection event
existing floor writer and Molnár comparison
halls.review_note: Array/tutorial.md is still absent. The reduced learner study and its display connection need choosing before a full lesson. The row uses array_data[0][i]; the grid uses grid_data[x][z]. Molnár’s current data is a different retained structure, not this occupancy table. Do not present Grid’s earlier lossy snapping as reversible.
halls.independent_check: Empty a chosen slot, then change the spacing. Predict which stored value changes and explain why neither operation renumbers the neighbours.
halls.critical_question: The address survives an absence. What does the stored zero leave unexplained?
halls.change_reason: Make row-to-grid addressing the main lesson. Move stored random departures from a second required concept into an optional return; retain the floor writer’s bodily consequences without teaching a floor-editing system.

halls.title: Name the layer and keep the convention visible
halls.storyboard: In the flight enclosure, the student selects a cube above the ground and later reads zero where it stood. They bring the two-index occupancy record and extend the study to layers. The displayed address is [x, y, z], while the installed volume reads values[y][z][x]. Before changing a value, they show how the earlier [x][z] plane becomes one [z][x] layer: the conversion is part of the lesson. Flight, selection and collection are supplied. The student predicts an unequal-index address, changes its value and reads it back without shifting its neighbours. They carry an explicit storage-to-space mapping. Open structures and suspended fragments remain further uses of addressed places, not additional required data systems.
halls.storyboard_short: Use flight enclosure. Reuse occupancy record. Teach displayed [x,y,z] → values[y][z][x]; explicitly convert earlier [x][z] plane into a [z][x] layer. Supply flight/selection/collection. Check unequal indices; write/read one slot without shifts. Carry storage-to-space mapping. Open structures/suspension remain comparisons. Open: reduced study binding; an added dimension grants no flight.
learns: three-index addressing
explicit conversion between storage conventions
halls.carries: An explainable mapping from displayed XYZ to stored layer/row/entry
halls.review_note: Wrapping the earlier grid directly would yield values[y][x][z], not the installed values[y][z][x]. Explain the conversion or a named reader explicitly. The installed enclosure is four by four by four; the learner study may be smaller. Current tutorial’s open-form edits do not yet teach this storage conversion.
halls.independent_check: Predict the place at [1, 2, 0], identify values[2][0][1], change that entry and retrieve it. Explain why spacing and flight permission are separate from the three indices.
halls.critical_question: Which places can the record name, and which can a body actually reach?
halls.change_reason: Replace the generic layer/row/column description with the actual XYZ-to-YZX relationship. Expose the change from the earlier grid instead of hiding a transpose inside supplied code.

halls.title: Let an address choose a turn
halls.storyboard: At the paired four-by-four samples, one extra turn at each address makes a larger figure cross the joints. The student brings addressing and rotation, but now gives the value another declared meaning: zero quarter-turns is an orientation, not an empty slot. With the asymmetric tile and image renderer supplied, they write one address-to-turn function using remainder by four. They predict a selected tile’s result, then add one exceptional address. Enlarging the field repeats the same calculation without adding instructions. They carry the motif choice, turn rule and exception separately. The other fields provide comparisons; the floor’s apparent ridges do not become steps underfoot.
halls.storyboard_short: Use paired 4×4 samples. Reuse indices/rotation. Teach address → quarter-turn via remainder; zero means orientation, not vacancy. Supply motif/image renderer. Predict one result, add one exception, enlarge field with same rule. Carry motif + turn rule + exception. Other fields compare. Existing tiling rasterizes images; no per-tile body or stored occupancy implied. Open: learner-rule binding.
learns: address-to-orientation function
remainder and one exceptional address
new value meaning requires a declared reader
halls.carries: A motif and an address-to-turn rule with one explicit exception
supplied: image renderer and existing rule-comparison controls
halls.review_note: The installed floor makes raster images from a rule; it is not a nested table of colliding triangle tiles. Do not require the learner to rebuild the renderer. The current tutorial redirects to final.md, so this remains a teaching selection rather than an implemented companion.
halls.independent_check: Predict a turn at an address you have not inspected. Keep one exception, then enlarge the field and explain why the local rule needs no extra clauses.
halls.critical_question: When a larger figure appears across the joints, where does the work of the small rule end?
halls.change_reason: State the change from occupancy to orientation. Use the existing four-by-four study for a prediction, one exception and a larger field; make its image renderer an explicit supplied component.

halls.title: Keep the pattern, change what carries it
halls.storyboard: The same pattern now stands in front of the student. They bring the motif and turn rule from the floor and reuse its generated image on a supplied upright receiver. The eye chart and a walk toward and away from it let them compare what remains legible as its apparent size changes. No new syntax is needed. At the exception wall, they predict the difference between turning a mark inside the image and turning the sheet with its collision. One alters the picture; the other can open a passage. The hinge and finite landing stay supplied. They carry a comparison separating source, appearance and access, including the brief chance to look back at the outside of the museum’s enclosure.
halls.storyboard_short: Use wall fields, eye chart and turning wall. Reuse floor motif/rule/image on supplied upright receiver. Compare distance and apparent scale; no new syntax. Predict image-turn versus carrier/collision-turn. Supply hinge/landing. Carry source–appearance–access distinction. Preserve the outside pause. Open: learner image assignment; no new tiling or wall-construction lesson.
brings: generated image and a declared receiver
learns: same image with a different receiver
image change versus physical passage
halls.carries: A reusable image and a comparison of source, appearance and access
supplied: upright image receiver and eye chart
hinged wall, collision handling and finite landing
halls.review_note: Reuse of the learner’s own generated image needs an explicit assignment; the installed floor and walls already share a generator, not an automatically transported learner record. Preserve the mature main text and the wall’s collision/safety behavior.
halls.independent_check: Before using either control, predict which turn could open a route and explain why changing the image alone cannot do so. Keep the same image while comparing floor and wall.
halls.critical_question: What was the thin enclosure doing for our forward walk, before we saw its other side?
halls.change_reason: Give the floor’s image a concrete return on another receiver. Preserve the eye chart and exterior landing as a reflective pause instead of adding another construction exercise.

halls.title: Let a clock read the choices you kept
halls.storyboard: The monochrome floor changes while a separate sequencer offers empty cells to fill. The student brings indexed lookup, remainder and elapsed time. They make a short score with explicitly named track and step indices, following the instrument’s [track][step] convention; false means no new sound trigger, not a missing floor tile. A supplied sound receiver handles the note. The student advances a playhead through the kept score, moves an event without changing tempo, then changes tempo without rewriting the entries. They stop the score and watch the floor continue. They carry a reusable timed reader. The sixteen-step score’s connection to twelve floor columns is a comparison of addresses, not a lesson in recording footsteps.
halls.storyboard_short: Use separate sequencer and changing floor. Reuse lookup/remainder/time. Teach score[track][step] plus timed playhead; false = no new trigger. Supply sound receiver/display. Move event at fixed tempo; change tempo with score fixed; stop score and predict floor. Carry timed reader. 16 steps/12 columns can share a flash address. No footstep recording. Open: old tutorial contradicts current encounter.
learns: stored events read by a separate clock
track/step addressing
inactive event versus absent geometry
halls.carries: A kept score and an independently controlled timed reader
supplied: existing sequencer display and independently animated floor
halls.review_note: The current instrument stores four tracks by sixteen boolean steps; the floor has twelve columns. The learner can start with one short track. The companion still describes a 17×17 footstep-recording floor, undefined supplied pieces and deferred Chamber_Arrays. This summary pass does not repair that full lesson: rewrite it from the present score before presenting it as reliable instructions.
halls.independent_check: Move an event while tempo stays fixed, then alter tempo without changing any entry. Stop the score and predict which floor behavior continues. As a further comparison, explain why step 0 and step 12 can flash the same floor column.
halls.critical_question: What changes when you move with a rhythm but the system does not record your steps?
halls.change_reason: Make the score’s value meaning and reader explicit, keep the independent clocks, and give the student an observable variation. Flag the old 17×17 footstep-recording tutorial as unresolved rather than silently treating its code as current.

status: Revised teaching proposal; full companion repairs and learner adapters remain pending

arc: PROPOSED. Colour returns to the forms, transforms and addressed assignments already available. Keep geometry while changing its palette; keep a surface while moving its light. Nails introduces one bounded position-to-colour function and an explained receiver. Pillar changes that function’s coordinate convention; Grid keeps a returned value at an address. Paint returns to an existing timed path on an evolving image. Walls carries palette and arrangement onward into Tiling. Rainbow remains a generous pause with optional palette-making. Equal values need not look alike; these proposed learner connections do not imply automatic transport between exhibits.

halls.title: Let colour regroup an assembly
halls.storyboard: The first columns keep the same five forms while their colour assignments change. Bringing primitives, transforms and array lookup, the student selects colours for a small supplied part list while keeping its geometry fixed. Begin with list position; supplied numeric shape categories offer a second grouping once that assignment is clear. Each part has an explained material reference, so choosing a palette entry and assigning it are visible operations. The student regroups two separated parts by colour without moving either. They carry a palette and a selection rule independent of placement. The larger stacks, historical associations and cone landscape remain available for looking and composition without becoming additional required builds.
halls.storyboard_short: Use fixed-geometry columns. Reuse primitives/transforms/lookup. Teach palette selection separately from material assignment and placement. Supply part/material references; numeric categories optional after index selection. Check: regroup separated parts without moving them. Carry palette + selection rule. Rich stacks remain encounters. Open: reduced host binding; no dictionary lesson assumed.
learns: palette selection separate from placement
a colour value assigned to a named material
halls.carries: A palette and a selection rule, with a declared material receiver.
supplied: existing part geometry with direct material references
halls.review_note: Use a small explicit part/category list before requiring dictionaries. The museum’s richer stack records remain supplied; choose the reduced editing entry before writing a full lesson.
halls.independent_check: Give two separated parts the same colour without changing their positions; explain which selection changed.
halls.change_reason: Keep the opening focused on how colour regroups familiar parts.

halls.title: Change what reaches a surface
halls.storyboard: The student moves a coloured lamp across the pale board and faceted sphere, then follows the source edit already offered by this hall. They bring material colour and transforms and keep a direct reference to one existing supplied light. Change its colour while leaving the receiving surface alone; then keep the colour and change the lamp’s direction. Predict which condition changed before comparing the result. The fixed lamp in the side room offers a later return to time-varying colour. Grabbing, room geometry and the renderer remain supplied. The student carries a controllable light and the distinction between a value assigned to a material and light reaching it; no new room or lamp assembly is required.
halls.storyboard_short: Use existing lamp/board/faceted sphere. Reuse colour assignment and transforms. Follow current bounded light-colour edit; retain named light reference. Vary colour with receiver fixed, then aim with colour fixed. Supply grabbing/room/renderer. Carry illumination versus albedo distinction. Timed lamp optional. No new room; no spectral-optics claim.
learns: light colour and aim as different inputs to appearance
halls.carries: An explained existing light reference and a controlled comparison of receiving conditions.
halls.review_note: The existing tutorial already provides a small light-colour edit. Retain that entry; do not replace it with a new host or require lighting equations.
halls.independent_check: Choose another light colour, predict its effect on an unchanged surface, then vary aim alone.
halls.change_reason: The existing encounter already provides the necessary experiment.

halls.title: Use a position to choose a colour
halls.storyboard: The held point recolours nails on the giant and petite hands and, in the standard VR setup, the choosing hand. Reuse a position in a named local frame and bounded mapping. The student writes one function taking that local position and positive box dimensions, clamping each component to the box and dividing by its dimension: X becomes red, Y green, Z blue. It returns a Color; one named preview material receives it through albedo_color. The grab connection, hand meshes and application signals are supplied. Predict the colour at a different point and revisit it, then keep nail colour fixed while changing rendered skin. Carry the function and a recorded colour. Preserve the critical distinction between these equally easy assignments and their unequal lived meanings.
halls.storyboard_short: Use RGB point and salon hands. Reuse local position/bounded mapping. Teach positive box sizes; clamp/divide X→R, Y→G, Z→B; return Color → named preview albedo. Supply grabbing/hands/signals. Predict another point, revisit it; keep nails fixed while changing skin. Carry function + recorded colour. Preserve Lorde/embodied difference. Open: reduced preview binding; no automatic Rainbow transfer.
brings: held position in a declared local frame
learns: local box coordinates normalised to RGB
returned colour value versus receiving material
halls.carries: A bounded RGB function and a recorded result that can be reused deliberately.
supplied: grab connection and positive box dimensions
preview material, hand meshes and application signal route
halls.review_note: The current companion offers observation/source tracing, not this complete authored function. Bind the reduced function to one named preview before expanding the lesson. GameManager already retains hand/nail choices, but that does not feed Rainbow or Grid automatically. Preserve the main text’s Lorde passage.
halls.independent_check: Predict the RGB result at a new local point, revisit it, then apply that value to the declared preview without changing the hand geometry.
halls.change_reason: Give the student a reusable operation without making the salon a wiring lesson.

halls.title: Divide one span into chosen colours
halls.storyboard: RE-DIVIDE changes the bands while the opening and celebration remain available. Bring the palette list and a colour recorded at Nails; there is no automatic transfer. An optional making step substitutes that value in a hand-picked palette, then compares different nonempty palette lengths with the same total band width. The curved-strip builder is supplied with radius, width and colour inputs and a returned strip reference; the learner can inspect the fixed-width division without rebuilding the arch. Predict which boundaries move while the opening stays. The forty-eight-band version introduces the difference between many samples and continuity. Carry palette choice and partitioning onward. Staying, looking and celebrating can complete this hall without another coding assignment.
halls.storyboard_short: Use RE-DIVIDE; celebration stays unconditional. Reuse palette; manually record/reuse Nails colour. Optional: replace palette entry, compare nonempty lengths at fixed total width. Supply curved-strip builder and route. Predict seams versus opening. Carry palette/partition distinction. Many bands remain discrete; HSV sampler optional before Pillar. No automatic transfer or optics claim.
learns: optional fixed-span partition by nonempty palette length
halls.carries: A chosen palette and an understanding of what its partition preserves.
supplied: existing arch, celebration and accessible route
curved-strip builder; optional supplied HSV palette
halls.review_note: Keep making optional. The installed options are six, seven, forty-eight and two bands. A hand-picked palette avoids making HSV a prerequisite here. Celebration does not require completing a task.
halls.independent_check: If taking the making route, choose another nonempty palette and predict which band boundaries move while the total span stays fixed.
halls.change_reason: Preserve the room’s generosity and avoid treating every artwork as homework.

halls.title: Ask a field for a colour
halls.storyboard: A moving card samples the field between the pillars; leaving it in place keeps its latest sample. Bring Nails’ position-to-colour function and change the rule explicitly: X now chooses hue, Z saturation and represented Y value, converted with Color.from_hsv. The supplied height adapter maps the card’s local 0.65–1.85 metre range into the field’s 0.46–4.60 metre height; it is not the same position passed unchanged. Predict a sample between columns, then vary height while keeping the other coordinates. At value zero, different addresses yield the same black. Carry the field function and one recorded result toward Grid. The matching ceiling and named swatches remain encounters with appearance, classification and the gaps between visible samples.
halls.storyboard_short: Use moving sampler and constant swatch. Reuse Nails function pattern, change convention: field X→H, Z→S, Y→V; convert HSV→Color. Supply explicit hand-height adapter (.65–1.85 → .46–4.60 m), card/readouts. Predict between columns; vary V alone. Movement resamples; stationary card keeps latest. Carry function + recorded result. Black has many source addresses; HSV is not perceptually uniform. No automatic Grid handoff.
brings: declared reference frame and bounded ranges
learns: HSV mapping and conversion
input adaptation versus field evaluation
rule versus displayed samples
halls.carries: A stated colour-field function and one recorded sample for an addressed write.
halls.review_note: The sampler checks position each frame, not whether it is held. A released stationary card keeps the last sample because its position stops changing. Use actual ranges from hsv_at; value is not perceived lightness. A recorded result or copied function can connect Grid, but the installed exhibits have no such transfer.
halls.independent_check: Predict a sample between columns; raise represented height alone, then explain why black cannot reveal its unique source address.
halls.change_reason: Make the change of representation teachable without claiming one formula serves both rooms unchanged.

halls.title: Let one address keep a colour
halls.storyboard: The outline leaves an edited square and returns to find its colour. Bring array addressing and a recorded result from Nails or Pillar. In the proposed reduced study, write that colour to one chosen address through an explained address-to-instance receiver; selecting another address must not write to either. The installed console instead cycles four inks, so using the learner’s own value is a proposed binding. Revisit the address, then apply the whole-grid rule and predict the replacement. Carry stored assignment separately from live field evaluation. Preserving one exception is an optional later policy, not current behaviour. The wider reach of RULE, the twenty-five selectable sites and the unbroken floor retain their critical force.
halls.storyboard_short: Use edited floor square. Reuse address/lookup and recorded Nails/Pillar Color. Propose write through named address→instance receiver; selection only reads. Check leave/return, then predict RULE overwrite. Current COLOUR cycles four inks; custom input needs binding. Carry stored assignment versus live evaluation. Optional protected exception; no history/current protection. Keep 25-site control versus wider rule and unchanged support.
brings: colour returned by an earlier function
learns: selection versus assignment
stored sample versus live evaluation
explicit overwrite policy
halls.carries: A colour value stored at an address and a known rule for replacing it.
halls.review_note: Vector2i.y denotes room Z here. The actual colour is a MultiMesh instance value, not one separate material per cell. Current COLOUR cycles INKS; custom function input is proposed. RULE overwrites mapped floor colours; protected exceptions/history are not implemented.
halls.independent_check: Write a recorded colour to one address, leave and return without modifying it, then predict what RULE will replace. The custom-colour binding remains to be supplied.
halls.change_reason: Make the strongest sequence handoff concrete while distinguishing the proposed input from the installed four inks.

halls.title: Give a mark somewhere to remain
halls.storyboard: The automatic can is painting before the student takes a manual one. Bring elapsed time, sine and the distinction between an address and the value kept there. Read the existing two-coordinate automatic path, then change one rate or amplitude while keeping the other coordinate unchanged. Predict whether the path becomes narrower or turns at another pace. The supplied host converts surface coordinates into a hit and sends deposits to the same draw_spray operation used by the manual cans. Compare a quick pass with staying in one place. Carry the path rule and the distinction between replacing a grid entry and contributing to an image that spreads and fades. The shader and spray apparatus remain supplied; no second brush is required.
halls.storyboard_short: Use existing automatic path/manual cans. Reuse time/sine/address distinctions. Edit one UV rate or amplitude; predict path width or pace with other coordinate fixed. Supply UV→hit mapping and shared draw_spray surface. Compare quick versus repeated deposits. Carry path rule and evolving-image distinction, not recoverable gesture history. No second brush; defer spray/feedback shader. Albers remains an encounter.
learns: bounded two-coordinate surface path
deposit versus replacement
evolving image versus stored gesture list
halls.carries: An editable path and an explicit account of what the canvas keeps and changes.
supplied: existing automatic caller and surface-coordinate conversion
shared spray operation, ray hits and evolving-image renderer
halls.review_note: Both automatic and manual callers already reach draw_spray. Keep that shared operation rather than proposing another brush system. Its retained image spreads and fades; it is not permanent storage or a lossless list of strokes. UVs are introduced as two bounded surface coordinates; shader implementation comes later.
halls.independent_check: Change one amplitude without changing either rate; predict the path’s extent, then compare a faster pass with repeated deposits at a place.

Contacts and measurements are supplied. The clock-driven forge and restarting optimiser provide contrasting arrivals to inspect. No new syntax is required; the learner carries a declared criterion and can distinguish meeting it from becoming alive or finding a universally best form.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the quiet low stack failing height requirements. Reuse timers, conditions and physical/prescribed distinctions. Write height-and-low-movement-duration success criteria; test a rejected construction. Supply contacts and measurements. Carry a declared criterion without new syntax or claims of life/universal optimality. Compare restarting optimiser and clock-driven forge. Open: measurement interface; MAX Q is a clock effect, not an optimisation measure.
learns: authored success criteria
halls.carries: A tested criterion stated separately from the physical result.
halls.review_note: Confirm the small measurement interface before expanding code. The forge's MAX Q is clock-driven and must not become an optimisation measurement.

arc: Sine returns as something already usable, now examined through state, sampling, circular coordinates, spatial form and sound. The student contrasts a computed swing with a prescribed cycle, constructs a wave through neighbouring interactions, and separates a sound event from the signal it starts. The final harmonic sum recombines functions and arrays while making the limits of its chosen vocabulary available for the coming study of randomness.

halls.title: The same angle can carry another motion
halls.storyboard: The released pendulum crosses the ring twice with opposite velocity signs. Bringing the spring's state update and vector projection, the student makes a small angular model using a supplied restoring-acceleration rule, then compares releases from the same angle with different initial angular velocities. The bob, constrained hold and hand-velocity samples are supplied; projecting the release along the swing gives one deliberate input. Nearby sine-driven cubes provide the contrast with prescribed motion. The learner leaves with an angular state model and can explain why position alone does not determine what happens next.
halls.storyboard_short: Use opposite-velocity pendulum crossings and prescribed sine cubes. Reuse spring integration and dot projection. Teach angle/angular-velocity state; project hand release along swing and compare equal angles with different velocities. Supply bob, constrained hold, hand samples and restoring-acceleration rule. Carry angular state beyond position alone. Open: timestep and damping; current texts identify frame-dependent damping.
learns: angular state and release velocity
halls.carries: A pendulum state with angle and angular velocity.
halls.review_note: Resolve the teaching model's timestep and damping before code expansion; current source texts identify a frame-dependent damping regime.

halls.title: Keep when as well as where
halls.storyboard: A teal mark recedes behind the pendulum while the bob returns. The student brings Trace's ordered positions and now records a named position and timestamp for each sample, then draws age along a separate axis. The pendulum and drawing receiver are supplied; the learner owns sampling interval, count limit and age limit. Comparing a fine record, a coarse one and sampling near one whole period shows that an unchanged motion can leave very different evidence. The reusable outcome is a bounded timestamped recorder, with its display direction distinguished from the body's actual path.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the pendulum's receding teal record. Reuse Trace and elapsed time. Teach named position/timestamp fields, sampling interval and count/age bounds; draw age on a separate axis. Compare fine, coarse and near-period sampling. Supply pendulum state and renderer. Carry a bounded timestamped recorder with temporal resolution/span. Keep display direction separate from body path; do not silently encode time in position components.
learns: timestamped records
sampling and memory limits
halls.carries: A recorder that states its temporal resolution and retained span.
halls.review_note: Introduce named fields for position and time explicitly. Do not reuse a Vector3 position component as time without explaining that changed data contract.

halls.title: Make a wave into a surface
halls.storyboard: Spheres meet the tray's folds, while the corridor's moving walls offer a different relation to the visitor. Bringing indexed geometry and the early sine function, the student samples two spatial sines on a small grid, multiplies them into heights and joins neighbouring samples with known triangles. A supplied mesh-to-collision step gives the static tray a physical boundary; sphere release and counting remain supplied. They compare surface relief with body size before the observation window ends. The reusable result is a sampled height surface, with spatial frequency, visible geometry and physical contact kept distinct.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the tray and collision-disabled corridor walls. Reuse grid samples, triangles and sine. Multiply two spatial sines into grid heights; join neighbours. Supply static mesh-to-collision creation, sphere release and counts. Compare relief with body size within the observation window. Carry a sampled height field distinguishing spatial frequency, visible surface and contact. Defer moving construction until mesh/collision updates are explained.
learns: spatial wave sampling
mesh versus physical boundary
halls.carries: A sine height field with explicit collision provision.
halls.review_note: The corridor walls have collision disabled. Keep the student construction static until a later lesson explains updating both mesh and collision.

halls.title: Build the circular sampler
halls.storyboard: The rotating point supplies two projections, and the graph keeps a history of one of them. Reusing the sine cycle and pivoted construction, the student writes the circular position function that earlier lessons supplied: cosine and sine give the two offsets, radius scales them, and the centre places them. The reference circle, angle control and graph receiver are supplied. Quarter-turn predictions establish radians, phase and the relation between both coordinates. The learner replaces a borrowed circle sampler with an understood generator, while recognising that one projection alone cannot recover the whole position.
halls.storyboard_short: Use rotating point, two projections and graph. Reuse sine and pivot/radius. Teach centre plus radius-scaled cosine/sine; predict quarter turns to establish radians/phase. Supply circle, angle control and graph receiver. Carry an understood sampler replacing those supplied in Primitives and curved strips. One projection cannot recover full position; do not generalise uniform rotation to all periodic motion.
learns: sine and cosine as circular coordinates
radians and phase
halls.carries: An understood circle sampler and its projections.
halls.review_note: Return explicitly to the sampler supplied in Primitives and curved-strip construction; do not claim all periodic motion is a projection of uniform rotation.

halls.title: Let neighbours transmit a disturbance
halls.storyboard: In the existing museum lattice, compare a local pulse with coupling on and off. Carry PointBody and LineSkin from Unit Circle into nine points with displacement and velocity arrays. Raise the centre, read all forces from the same old state, then commit the next state. Predict the first neighbours to respond, preserve symmetry and compare seven points and half the initial height. Carry local transmission into the next hall's contrast with prescribed phase modulation.
halls.storyboard_short: Museum lattice: PULSE; compare COUPLED/INDEPENDENT from reset. Carry PointBody/LineSkin. Build 9 vertical oscillators; raised centre; old/next arrays; adjacent displacement force. Predict first step; test symmetry and zero coupling. Transfer: 7 points, half height. Print all construction. Museum gives host only. Distinguish 1D release, 2D pulse and analytic tile field. Next: phase modulation.
brings: PointBody and LineSkin from Unit Circle
learns: neighbour displacement differences contribute force
all points read old state before commit
finite ends have fewer neighbours
halls.carries: A coupled oscillator row with explicit update order.
supplied: museum player, camera, lighting and floor
halls.review_note: Canonical tutorial/final revised; exact printed code passes 28 checks and rejects three faults. 54 native museum checks. Full code constructs its own marker display and readout; no hidden scene objects. See 2026-10-08-wave-propagation-between-points. Review draft; no headset or independent student validation.

halls.title: Put one oscillation inside another
halls.storyboard: At the two desks, the held note makes a change of the orange ball audible beside its baseline. The student brings sampled functions and sine, then fills a short list of sound samples with a carrier whose phase receives a second sine. A supplied buffer encoder and player turn the list into a note; the amplitude envelope and audition controls are supplied with their roles stated. They keep carrier frequency fixed while comparing modulation depth. The reusable outcome is a small signal function, with modulation inside phase distinguished from simply adding another audible tone.
halls.storyboard_short: Use two desks and held-note comparison. Reuse sampled functions and sine phase. Fill a finite sample list with a carrier receiving a second sine inside phase; hold frequency while varying depth. Supply encoding, playback, envelope and audition controls. Carry phase modulation distinct from tone addition. Open: responsive note length and desktop input; the scope does not prove listening experience.
learns: phase modulation
audio samples as a finite signal
halls.carries: A carrier-plus-modulator sample function.
halls.review_note: Choose a responsive teaching note length and provide a real desktop input path. The existing scope is not proof of the listener's experience.

halls.title: Read time through a static form
halls.storyboard: A ridge twists upward while its whole column slowly turns. Bringing the circle sampler and height-field construction, the student builds a short stack of rings whose angular offset depends on height, then connects corresponding corners using their known face construction. Lighting and a reference column are supplied. They pause their whole-object rotation to inspect the twist that remains, then restore it without rebuilding the profile. The learner carries a height-dependent geometry generator and a clear distinction between a form varying through space and that completed form changing through time.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the twisting, rotating column. Reuse circle sampling and connected faces. Build a reduced ring stack beside it with angular offset depending on height; connect corresponding corners. Pause/restart whole-object rotation without rebuilding geometry. Supply reference column and lighting. Carry spatial twist distinct from temporal animation. Open: source-check reduced geometry; avoid the old incomplete triangle-strip construction.
learns: height-dependent twist
halls.carries: A ring-based twisted form independent of its animation.
halls.review_note: Use a reduced shaft beside the exhibit; its geometry should be source-checked instead of repeating the old tutorial's incomplete triangle-strip construction.

halls.title: Compose what chance may choose
halls.storyboard: The student listens for a continuous layer and intermittent events, then attends to their intervals instead of counting every entrance. Bringing the early bounded random choice and timed score, they make a short event score from a supplied sound collection, explicitly choosing the available entries and interval bounds. Sound generation and playback are supplied. Replaying a kept event list distinguishes the decisions that composed a vocabulary from the choices that arranged one performance. No new syntax is necessary. The reusable outcome is an inspectable chance score that prepares the deeper Randomness sequence without claiming to perform a Cage work.
halls.storyboard_short: Use continuous sound and intermittent events; attend to intervals. Reuse bounded choice and timed scores. Propose a retained event list with chosen vocabulary/interval bounds; replay to distinguish authored options from performance choices. Supply sounds and playback. Carry inspectable chance composition toward Randomness without new syntax. Open: replay extension; current soundscape records no visitor sound and implements no particular Cage score.
learns: authored vocabulary versus selected performance
halls.carries: A retained chance score with stated options and timing bounds.
halls.review_note: A replayable teaching score is a proposed extension. The current soundscape neither records visitor sound nor implements a particular Cage score.

halls.title: Give each note its own beginning
halls.storyboard: A struck bar keeps ringing after the hand leaves; striking another adds a voice while restriking the first restarts it. The student brings the generated note and event-based state, then gives two supplied sound players separate start times and multiplies each sine by a decaying envelope. The striker detection, buffer encoder and bar bodies are supplied. They compare a retrigger with two overlapping notes and keep the chosen frequency independent of visible bar length. The reusable outcome is an event-driven voice whose age belongs to its own beginning, ready to combine with others.
halls.storyboard_short: Use ringing bars, retriggers and overlapping strikes. Reuse sine notes and event state. Give two supplied players separate start times; multiply each sine by a decaying envelope. Compare retrigger/overlap; keep chosen frequency independent of visible length. Supply strike events, bodies and encoding. Carry independently aged voices. Open: desktop strike input; the synthesised model does not derive frequency from material.
learns: per-voice time and decay
retrigger versus overlapping voices
halls.carries: Two independently started decaying voices.
halls.review_note: Use the current synthesised-bar model. A physical bar's frequency is not solved from its material, and desktop strike input must be made concrete.

halls.title: Turn sampled positions into support
halls.storyboard: The spiral's radius breathes while its treads rise steadily, and connecting surfaces fill some spaces between them. Bringing circular sampling, spatial sine and repeated bodies, the student constructs a short three-to-six-tread segment beside the existing stair. They calculate tread centres, then give each a width, orientation and separate collision boundary through supplied tread components. Comparing inner and outer edges exposes what centre spacing leaves undecided. The large staircase and its surrounding floor are supplied for inspection. The reusable outcome is a small route segment whose support is tested independently of the smooth formula behind its outline.
halls.storyboard_short: Use uniform rise and sine-modulated stair radius. Reuse circle sampling, spatial sine and repeated bodies. Build three-to-six treads beside the stair; calculate centres, widths, orientations and separate collision boundaries. Supply tread components, staircase and viewing floor. Compare inner/outer edges. Carry a tested support segment beyond centre spacing; do not infer complete climbing or headset comfort.
learns: sample placement versus usable support
halls.carries: A short stair segment with explicit tread provision.
halls.review_note: The active stair has uniform rise and sine-modulated radius. Do not claim a complete climb or headset comfort from the sampled segment.

halls.title: A slow envelope from two fast returns
halls.storyboard: At the three rows, A and B keep oscillating while their sum grows and shrinks more slowly. Bringing sine functions and independent rates, the student samples two close frequencies at the same times and adds their signed values into a third record. The row display and frequency controls are supplied; the learner states its drawing scale separately from the computed sum. They exchange which frequency is higher and predict the envelope's pace before running again. The reusable result is a two-signal comparison that reveals cancellation without inventing a third source or claiming the visual exhibit produces sound.
halls.storyboard_short: Use the three-row beat exhibit. Reuse sine, frequency and phase. Sample two close frequencies at shared times; add signed values into a third record with separate display scale. Supply rows and controls. Exchange higher frequency and predict envelope pace. Carry superposition/cancellation without a third source or audio claim. Keep walking paths secondary: finite and circulating, not endlessly generated.
learns: superposition and beats
halls.carries: A two-signal sum with separate component records.
halls.review_note: Keep the beat exhibit primary. The existing walking paths are finite and circulating, not generated endlessly beneath the visitor.

halls.title: Choose the parts of a wave
halls.storyboard: The five coloured rows can be removed until only one sine remains beneath the pale sum. Bringing signal addition, lists and loops, the student writes a function that visits a coefficient list and adds each weighted harmonic at one shared phase. The sliders, sample plot and held comparison are supplied. They predict the contribution at a marked address, build a chosen finite shape and state which changes its nonnegative coefficients cannot express. The reusable outcome is a compact wave recipe; the room-memory detour offers a separate comparison between repeating stored state and processing it again.
halls.storyboard_short: Use five harmonic rows and their pale sum. Reuse addition, lists and functions. Sum weighted harmonics from coefficients at shared phase; predict a marked sample and build a finite shape, naming nonnegative-coefficient limits. Supply sliders, plot and held comparison. Carry a wave recipe. Keep room-memory repeat/reprocess comparison separate; this visual bench neither shares specimen state nor generates its waveform's audio.
learns: finite harmonic synthesis
halls.carries: A coefficient-list wave generator with declared limits.
halls.review_note: This bench is visual. Do not imply it shares state with the other lab specimens or already turns the composed waveform into audio.
